items.concept_name: Every square is a sum of odd numbers
items.question_text: How many consecutive odd numbers, starting from 1, add up to 144?
items.answer_explanation: The sum of the first n odd numbers is n squared. 144 = 12 x 12, so n = 12. The distractor 72 is 144 divided by 2, which is the error of halving instead of taking a square root.
items.cognitive_demand: single-step inverse use of a stated rule

difficulty.reason: requires recognising that the count is the root, not the half

misconception.description: Halving the number instead of taking its square root.

items.concept_name: Every square is a sum of odd numbers
items.answer_explanation: There are 6 odd numbers, so the sum is 6 x 6 = 36. Adding them directly also gives 36.

difficulty.reason: count the terms and square the count

items.concept_name: Every square is a sum of odd numbers
items.question_text: The sum of the first 15 odd natural numbers is which square number?
items.answer_explanation: The sum of the first n odd numbers is n squared, so the answer is 15 x 15 = 225.
items.cognitive_demand: apply the rule to a larger n

difficulty.reason: the rule is stated in the chapter

items.concept_name: Finding a side from an area
items.question_text: The area of a square field is 169 square metres. What is the length of its side?
items.answer_explanation: Area of a square is side x side, so the side is the square root of 169, which is 13 because 13 x 13 = 169. The distractor 84.5 is half of 169 and 26 is twice 13.
items.cognitive_demand: inverse of squaring in a measurement context

difficulty.reason: a perfect square within the tables

misconception.description: Halving the area instead of taking its square root.

items.note: Grounded on Q113597, which asks the same thing for 441 cm2. NOTE: Q113597 is tagged to concept 31333 'Where the name comes from' in the database, which is a mis-tag -- it is a find-the-side item. This item is filed under 31346, the concept it actually tests.

items.question_text: Why is multiplying a number by itself called 'squaring' the number?
items.correct_answer: Because the area of a square is side times side, so multiplying a length by itself gives the area of the square drawn on it. The geometry gives the operation its name.
items.answer_explanation: The chapter derives the name from area: a square of side 5 has area 5 x 5 = 25, so 25 is called the square of 5.
items.mark_scheme: 1 mark for area of a square = side x side; 1 mark for linking the name to that geometry.
items.cognitive_demand: explain the origin of a term

items.question_text: Which of these is a perfect square?
items.answer_explanation: 64 = 8 x 8. The other three lie between squares: 48 and 72 and 80 sit between 36, 49, 64 and 81, and none is a product of a whole number with itself.
items.cognitive_demand: recognise a square from the tables

items.question_text: By what smallest whole number must 48 be multiplied to make the product a perfect square?
items.answer_explanation: 48 = 2 x 2 x 2 x 2 x 3. The twos pair up but the 3 is unpaired, so one more 3 is needed. 48 x 3 = 144 = 12 x 12.
items.cognitive_demand: prime factorise and find the unpaired factor

difficulty.reason: needs the pairing idea, not just recall

misconception.description: Multiplying by the smallest prime factor present rather than the unpaired one.

items.question_text: Which of the following can NOT be a perfect square?
items.answer_explanation: A perfect square never ends in 2, 3, 7 or 8. 2027 ends in 7, so it cannot be a square. The other three are 32 squared, 56 squared and 64 squared.
items.cognitive_demand: use the ending-digit test to rule out

difficulty.reason: the test must be applied, not the squares recalled

misconception.description: Believing any large even number can be a square, so testing size rather than final digit.

items.question_text: A whole number ends in 3. Which digit does its square end in?
items.answer_explanation: Only the units digit affects the units digit of the product, and 3 x 3 = 9. For example 13 squared is 169 and 23 squared is 529.

items.question_text: Use the split (40 + 1) to find 41 squared.
items.mark_scheme: 1 mark for setting out the three terms; 1 mark for 1681.

difficulty.reason: three terms must be produced and added

misconception.description: Omitting the middle term 2ab and answering 1601.

items.question_text: What is the digit in the units place of 63 squared?
items.answer_explanation: The units digit of the square depends only on the units digit of the number, and 3 x 3 = 9. In full, 63 squared is 3969.

items.question_text: Find the value of x so that (8, 15, x) is a Pythagorean triplet, where x is the largest member.
items.answer_explanation: 8 squared + 15 squared = 64 + 225 = 289, and 289 = 17 x 17, so x = 17. The distractor 289 is the sum of the squares without taking the square root.
items.cognitive_demand: sum two squares and take a root

difficulty.reason: two steps, and the final root is outside the usual tables

misconception.description: Giving the sum of the squares as the answer instead of its square root.

items.question_text: Show that (7, 24, 25) is a Pythagorean triplet.
items.correct_answer: 7 squared + 24 squared = 49 + 576 = 625, and 25 squared = 625, so the three numbers form a Pythagorean triplet.
items.answer_explanation: A triplet needs the sum of the squares of the two smaller numbers to equal the square of the largest. 49 + 576 = 625 = 25 squared.
items.mark_scheme: 1 mark for computing 49 + 576 = 625; 1 mark for stating 25 squared = 625 and concluding.
items.cognitive_demand: verify a definition on given numbers

difficulty.reason: requires both squares and a comparison

items.question_text: Starting from 81 and subtracting 1, then 3, then 5 and so on, how many subtractions bring the result to zero?
items.answer_explanation: 81 = 9 x 9, and because the sum of the first n odd numbers is n squared, exactly 9 subtractions are needed. Checking: 81-1=80, -3=77, -5=72, -7=65, -9=56, -11=45, -13=32, -15=17, -17=0.
items.cognitive_demand: connect the subtraction count to the root

difficulty.reason: the shortcut must be seen, or nine steps carried out

misconception.description: Dividing by 2 and answering 40, treating the process as repeated halving.

items.note: Grounded on Q113575. NOTE: Q113575 asks about zeros in the square of 400 and is tagged to 31348 in the database, which is a mis-tag -- it is an ending-digits item. This item is filed under 31348, the concept it genuinely tests.

items.question_text: Repeated subtraction of odd numbers from a square number reaches zero after exactly 6 subtractions. What was the number?
items.answer_explanation: The number of subtractions equals the square root, so the number is 6 x 6 = 36.

difficulty.reason: the relation must be used backwards

items.concept_name: How many digits the root will have
items.question_text: A perfect square has 4 digits. How many digits does its square root have?
items.answer_explanation: Grouping the digits in pairs from the right gives two groups for a 4-digit number, and the root has one digit per group, so 2. For example the root of 1089 is 33.

difficulty.reason: the rule is stated in the chapter

items.concept_name: How many digits the root will have
items.question_text: How many digits will the square root of a 5-digit perfect square have?
items.answer_explanation: Pairing from the right, 5 digits give three groups (the leftmost group holding a single digit), so the root has 3 digits. For example the root of 10201 is 101.
items.cognitive_demand: apply the pairing rule to an odd digit count

difficulty.reason: the odd-length case is the one learners get wrong

misconception.description: Halving the digit count and answering 2 for a 5-digit number.
